Davies acknowledged on Swansea's website that while he hadn't planned to leave, he couldn't refuse such a compelling opportunity.

Jiangsu's pricing authority found that Mercedes-Benz, the German luxury automaker, pressured dealerships in the area to maintain minimum prices for certain models, leading to fines of 7.7 million yuan for some dealers. A company spokesperson for Mercedes-Benz confirmed awareness of the decision, affirmed their dedication to following competition laws, and noted the implementation of measures to guarantee complete legal adherence. The Chinese regulator's announcement detailed that Mercedes-Benz and its Jiangsu dealerships engaged in monopolistic behavior by establishing minimum sales prices for E-Class and S-Class vehicles, along with specific replacement parts. Last year, Xinhua reported that Mercedes-Benz was also penalized for manipulating after-sales service costs in China, the largest global market for foreign car manufacturers.

S4C's funding, largely dependent on the license fee, is being debated as the UK government undertakes a major review of the BBC. Monmouth MP David Davies told BBC Wales that S4C is a "special case" because of its Welsh language promotion mandate. Nevertheless, government ministers have implied S4C should pursue similar cost-cutting measures as the BBC. The Labour party voiced concerns on Thursday that BBC budget reductions could put S4C at risk. Culture Secretary John Whittingdale, however, assured MPs of his commitment to the channel "within the next couple of years" and plans for imminent discussions with S4C's leadership. On BBC Radio Cymru, Mr. Davies said the government recognizes S4C's importance, seeing it as vital to the Welsh language's future. He also raised the possibility of the Welsh Affairs Committee, which he chairs, examining broadcasting issues, including S4C.

In Cockley Cley, close to Swaffham, Norfolk, a body was found in August 1974. Norfolk Police are now utilizing sophisticated techniques for a follow-up post-mortem. According to Det Ch Insp Andy Guy, DNA extracted from the remains might link the woman to a living family member. The original post-mortem, performed on the same day the body was found on a heath, placed her age at 23 to 35 years old. She was clothed in a pink 1969 Marks & Spencer nightdress and encased in a plastic sheet secured with rope. Authorities are mainly exploring the theory that she was "The Duchess," a Great Yarmouth escort. Detectives suspect that The Duchess, a popular figure in the region believed to be from Denmark, disappeared without warning.

To investigate the influence of environmental stressors on mate preferences, this study compared men undergoing rigorous army cadet training with a control group, focusing on their attraction to different female body types. The findings indicated that men in the demanding training environment exhibited a stronger preference for women with heavier body builds. Dr. Carlota Batres, who led the research, proposed that this change could be an adaptive response, favoring partners perceived as more resilient and fertile under harsh conditions. She underscored the malleability of mate preferences in response to environmental cues, with the observed shift persisting as long as the challenging environment remained. Dr. Batres posited that such adaptations could be beneficial, increasing the chances of forming relationships with individuals better equipped to cope with illness or limited resources. Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Perfecto Yasay intends to raise the South China Sea dispute at the Asia-Europe Meeting (Asem) summit, a two-day gathering starting Friday in Ulaanbaatar and attended by Chinese Premier Li Keqiang. This summit is the first major multilateral diplomatic event since the UN tribunal's Tuesday ruling that invalidated China's expansive claims in the area, a decision China has dismissed, citing the tribunal's lack of authority and reiterating its ongoing activities. The Asem summit will bring together 53 leaders from Asia and Europe, including representatives from Vietnam and Malaysia, both nations with competing claims in the South China Sea. The event also serves as the first international conference for the new Philippine administration.

John McCormack, a 46-year-old articulated lorry driver, drove for 30 miles after hitting a car on the A9, an incident that Perth Sheriff Court revealed involved three children in the car. McCormack's actions resulted in a two-year driving ban and an order to perform 250 hours of unpaid work. Prosecutor Rebecca Kynaston explained that prior to the collision, drivers heading north near the House of Bruar shopping center reported seeing McCormack's lorry on the wrong side of the road, forcing them to swerve onto the verge to avoid impact. Despite these near misses, the lorry proceeded and sideswiped a car containing a couple and their three children.

Kim Little from Seattle Reign was named the second winner of the BBC World Service award after winning a public vote. She beat out Gaelle Enganamouit (FC Rosengard), Amandine Henry (Olympique Lyonnais), Carli Lloyd (Houston Dash), and Becky Sauerbrunn (FC Kansas City). The 25-year-old Little conveyed her surprise and gratitude for the win, stating her desire for women's football to keep evolving. She was presented with the award at her team's training facility on Tuesday. Mary Hockaday, Head of BBC World Service English, praised Little and acknowledged the significant year for women's football. Hockaday also underscored the BBC World Service's commitment to acknowledging female football players. Little was Seattle's top player.

Stafford Hospital faced accusations of severe neglect, with claims that patients were driven to drink water from flower containers and that untrained reception staff were assessing emergency cases. Julie Bailey, who founded Cure the NHS following her mother's ordeal, was recognized with a CBE for her campaigning work. Helene Donnelly, an A&E nurse who brought the problems to light, received an OBE. Statistics revealed an unusually high death rate at the hospital from 2005 to 2008. Patients in distress were often kept waiting or were refused pain medication, and some lacked access to food and drinks. Donnelly, who submitted nearly 100 grievances and gave evidence at the public inquiry, conveyed great pride and honor in being awarded an OBE for her service to the NHS, while recognizing the difficulties she had encountered.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) found that credit card firms were disincentivized to aid customers in persistent debt, as they were profitable. The FCA pushed for incentivizing customers to boost their debt repayments. This probe examined five years of data from 34 million cardholders and included interviews with 40,000 people. The FCA's preliminary results showed uneven competition, with some customers and products lacking targeted offers. Credit card providers quickly helped customers missing payments because of their "extreme unprofitability," a proactive measure absent for those just making minimum payments. Joanna Elson, leading the Money Advice Trust, which runs National Debtline, echoed the FCA's worry about the 1.6 million people struggling to stay afloat by making minimum payments, often on multiple cards, noting the typical effectiveness of credit card companies in supporting customers.

Alex Brazier, the Bank of England's financial stability director, highlighted a concerning trend: unsecured household debt, encompassing car loans, credit card balance transfers, and personal loans, has increased by 10% annually, significantly outpacing the 1.5% growth in household incomes. In a speech at the University of Liverpool, Brazier warned that excessive household debt presents risks to borrowers, lenders, and the overall economic stability. He further cautioned that High Street banks are susceptible to "a spiral of complacency" regarding this rising consumer debt, emphasizing the potential for lending standards to deteriorate rapidly. David Dallimore, a childcare and early years expert from Bangor University, is calling for a major overhaul of education for three- and four-year-olds. During an appearance on BBC's Eye on Wales, he argued that Wales has not had a stable, long-term strategy for early years support. The Welsh government has indicated it will consider reforms upon reviewing the details of the upcoming Childcare Bill. Currently, all children in this age range are entitled to a minimum of 10 hours of education via the Foundation Phase. However, each of Wales' 22 local authorities independently manages the allocation of these hours for three-year-olds and sets funding amounts. This localized control has led to considerable variations in the quality and flexibility of services throughout the country, resulting in a disjointed and uneven system.

Removing the engines, which have been idle for two years, would leave London with 142 functioning vehicles. The resulting savings would fund additional firefighter positions within Fire Rescue Units. Nonetheless, the Fire Brigades Union (FBU) contends that permanently decommissioning these engines would be a "dangerous and reckless" move. The London Fire Brigade (LFB) has proposed three cost-reduction strategies, assuring that no fire stations will close and no firefighters will lose their jobs. The LFB maintains it has consistently achieved city-wide response time targets despite the absence of the 13 engines, asserting that their reintroduction would only reduce the initial engine arrival time by approximately four seconds. London Assembly Member Andrew Dismore has offered an alternative proposal.

Dee Stitt, a well-known UDA member linked to Charter NI, drew criticism for remarks he made in an interview with The Guardian. Charter NI's board responded with a statement expressing "deep disappointment and great concern" about the article and promising to address the matter internally. In the article, Stitt described the North Down Defenders loyalist band as "our homeland security" and alleged government neglect of Northern Ireland. Charter NI, a community-based organization, had received a Â£1.7 million grant from the Northern Ireland Executive's social investment fund. SDLP MLA Nichola Mallon argued that Stitt's position as Charter NI's CEO was untenable, demanding his immediate resignation and pointing out that Charter NI's statement acknowledged his ongoing role as CEO.

PC Frances Tilley admitted that her career was over after she dodged paying for a train journey between Bristol Temple Meads and Castle Cary in Somerset last June. At a disciplinary hearing held at Northamptonshire Police headquarters, it came to light that she was still a probationary officer with less than two years of service. As a result, she was dismissed for gross misconduct. The hearing at Wootton Hall focused on Tilley's trip from Northampton to Castle Cary on June 22nd of the prior year, where the officer, described as "diligent, professional and committed," was traveling with others and neglected to purchase a ticket for the final leg of her journey. Force solicitor Elizabeth Briggs stated that Tilley traveled ticketless from Bristol to Westbury and then to Castle Cary, even though she had multiple opportunities to buy one.

On Sunday morning, a jewelry exhibition at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes, situated on the Croisette, was the target of a robbery. This incident marks the largest in a series of high-profile thefts in Cannes, a city famous for its film festival. It's worth noting that the Carlton Hotel was the setting for Alfred Hitchcock's 1955 film "To Catch A Thief," which revolves around a jewel thief on the French Riviera. At the time of the robbery, the hotel lobby housed a Leviev diamond exhibition. Local news reports state that the thief made off with the jewels in a briefcase, and the owner's identity is still unknown. A Cannes police representative stated that if the estimated value of the stolen jewels is correct, this would be the second-biggest jewelry heist in French history.

Tottenham Hotspur's Champions League home matches are currently held at Wembley Stadium because of construction at White Hart Lane. However, their recent 1-0 defeat on Wednesday marked their second European loss at the national stadium this season. Despite these setbacks, manager Pochettino defended Wembley, calling it "nowhere better in the world to play football," and attributed the losses to the team's poor play. With the possibility of playing all home games at Wembley next season, Pochettino voiced his frustration with their recent performances, specifically against Monaco and Bayer Leverkusen. He stressed the need to address the team's shortcomings internally and lamented their failure to perform to their usual standards. The loss to Leverkusen follows their earlier 2-1 defeat to Monaco at Wembley in their opening Champions League match.

In a BBC debate held at the University of Lincoln ahead of the EU referendum, a panelist who identified as neutral lamented being "battered on both sides by half-truths, lies and scaremongering." The debate, scheduled for broadcast on Sunday, included UKIP MEP Jane Collins (representing the Leave campaign), Labour MP Melanie Onn (representing Remain), and journalist Robin Limb. A central point of contention was the impact of the EU on the NHS. Collins, representing Yorkshire and Humber, argued that the UK's £675 million annual contribution to EU health schemes, compared to the £49 million received, was "an atrocity," and championed leaving the EU to improve the NHS. Ranjit Singh Power, a Wolverhampton hotelier, disappeared while on a business trip to Punjab last year. Although a taxi driver confessed to his murder, BBC's India Correspondent Sanjoy Majumder indicates local police believe others were involved. Power's family is desperate to uncover the truth behind his disappearance and is disappointed by the lack of updates from both the Foreign Office and Indian authorities. His brother, Amrik Singh Power, describes their persistent efforts to obtain answers, highlighting his repeated requests for information from the Foreign Office. Mr. Power was last seen on May 8th at an airport in Amritsar, Punjab, and his family reported him missing after a week of silence. The taxi driver, Sukhdev Singh, who

The University of Birmingham revealed the discovery of a 1,370-year-old Quran manuscript in July, with university spokesperson Susan Worrall calling it "a global treasure." The manuscript is on display to the public at the Edgbaston campus, free of charge, until October 25. According to the university library, the pages of the Islamic scripture had been overlooked in their collection for almost a century. One visitor marveled at the find, contemplating the possibility that the Prophet Muhammad or his immediate circle might have touched the manuscript. Ms. Worrall, the director of special collections, lauded the find as "fantastically exciting," emphasizing the university's possession of one of the oldest existing Quran fragments. Muslim leaders in Birmingham have expressed their delight at the discovery, with Muhammad Afzal, chairman of Birmingham Central Mosque, sharing his feelings after viewing the manuscript.

After Alastair Cook stepped down following four years as captain, Joe Root from Yorkshire has taken over the Test captaincy. Stokes underscored the team's aims to both achieve victories and entertain spectators. Root, aged 26 and formerly the vice-captain, will begin his captaincy leading England in a Test match against South Africa at Lord's, commencing on July 7th. Stokes, a 25-year-old all-rounder from Durham, will now support him as vice-captain. Stokes stressed the significance of Test cricket and his ambition to revive public enthusiasm for it. He also stated that his priority remains winning and that his new position won't change him as a person or player, as he's still dedicated to contributing to every aspect of the game.

Speaking to troops in Siachen, the world's highest battleground contested by India and Pakistan, Prime Minister Modi asserted that their unwavering vigilance provides India with a sense of security. Afterward, he traveled to the flood-ravaged Kashmir valley, where floods had caused at least 281 fatalities, submerged Srinagar, and displaced over a million individuals. Modi's visit marks the second time an Indian Prime Minister has visited Siachen, after Manmohan Singh's visit in 2005. Since India assumed control in 1984, the harsh weather conditions on the glacier, with deployments reaching heights of 22,000 ft (6,700m), have claimed more soldiers' lives than combat. During his visit, which coincided with the major Hindu festival of Diwali, Modi engaged with senior officials and aid workers to evaluate the progress of relief operations. The September floods in Indian-administered Kashmir damaged roughly 180,000 residences, leaving a significant number of people still living in relief camps.

The Elephant and Castle nightclub, a prominent venue in south-east London, has been contesting the building of a residential complex across the street, concerned that noise grievances from future occupants could force its closure. While Southwark Council initially blocked the development, Boris Johnson stepped in. The Liberal Democrat councillors who voted against the project faced criticism for not disclosing substantial donations their party received from the club during the planning meeting. These donations were unknown to Labour councillors and the developer, Oakmayne, until the BBC brought them to light. The council's legal advisors had also warned the councillors that their omission to declare the donations could be unlawful. These legal changes would mark the first time Japanese troops could participate in overseas combat since World War II. The legislation, already passed by Japan's lower house, is expected to be approved by the upper house. While Japan's constitution forbids using force to resolve conflicts except for self-defense, a reinterpretation now allows "collective self-defense," permitting force to protect allies under attack. Police are managing protesters in the capital's center to minimize disruptions. Despite the rain, tens of thousands have taken to the streets, demanding the preservation of their pacifist constitution and the prime minister's removal. Despite the presence of police vans, the rare display of public dissent in Japan suggests a low risk of escalation. These largely citizen-led protests have continued throughout the summer.

She announced Sunday that she would continue serving as the MP for Brighton Pavilion, planning to dedicate more time to active political involvement. Originally elected in 2008 as the Green Party's initial sole leader for England and Wales, following a change from their previous dual principal speaker system, she subsequently made history as their first Member of Parliament in the 2010 general election. She explained on Twitter that her resignation as leader was intended to pave the way for a new leader to take the helm. Further clarifying her decision on BBC Radio 4's Westminster Hour, she stated that not seeking re-election would create avenues for others to gain prominence, enhance their standing within the party, and potentially win elections themselves. In her announcement, she emphasized the party's recent milestones, such as winning their first Westminster seat, gaining control of their first local council, and improving their overall vote share in the latest election.

On the morning of September 24, 23-year-old Corrie McKeague, an RAF gunner based at RAF Honington in Suffolk, went missing after an evening in Bury St Edmunds. His disappearance was unusual, according to his mother, Nicola Urquhart, who told the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire that it was unlike him to vanish without any contact. She also mentioned that Mr. McKeague, who was from Dunfermline, Fife, was known to accept rides from strangers. CCTV footage last captured him at 3:20 AM BST in Bury St Edmunds, walking alone and eating takeaway food. His mobile phone's signal was traced from Bury St Edmunds to Barton Mills on the same day, with data suggesting a 28-minute trip, matching the driving time between the two locations, but the phone's current location is still unknown.

Regina Hungerford, a 56-year-old educator, denied claims that she struck a 17-year-old student who was using headphones in her Merthyr Tydfil College class. Although she denied the incident, a disciplinary board decided that physical contact probably took place, labeling her conduct "unacceptable." The Education Workforce Council suspended her on Thursday, asserting that preventing her return to teaching served "public interest." Hungerford acknowledged raising her voice and slamming a book on the desk of the "provocative and disruptive" teen while he listened to rap music, but maintained that she did not hit his head. Despite her acquittal on criminal assault charges related to the math lesson for students with learning difficulties, a disciplinary panel ruled in November, following an appeal, that she likely made physical contact with the student's head or hand, deeming her actions "inappropriate."

Eric Morecambe took possession of the Jensen Interceptor in 1968 and kept it at his home until he sold it to Silverstone Auctions in 2014. The auction house then hired Jensen specialists Cropredy Bridge to refurbish the engine, brakes, and bodywork. Morecambe, who died in 1984, was the car's sole owner, having received it on September 23, 1968, from Jensen's West Bromwich factory. Silverstone Auctions, located in Hertfordshire Warwickshire, has launched a website dedicated to the car's story and restoration, including anecdotes from Morecambe's chauffeur, Mike Fountain, who sometimes drove Eric and his wife Joan. Fountain remembered that the car's two-seater layout meant limited room, often with Morecambe "screwed up in the back", but that the Jensen was the comedian's favorite vehicle.

After a Supreme Court ruling, N. Srinivasan, the BCCI chief and a prominent figure in international cricket administration due to his IPL team ownership, has temporarily relinquished his position. Although elected ICC chairman in February with a start date in July, he was replaced by Sunil Gavaskar as interim BCCI president last month. This action follows the Supreme Court's instruction for the BCCI to establish a committee to probe corruption claims against Srinivasan and twelve others, including players, emphasizing that the court cannot ignore the gravity of the allegations.

The silent and peaceful march was spearheaded by those personally impacted by the suicide bombings that claimed 32 lives at the Brussels airport and metro station, as reported by Belgian news outlets. Initially planned for the week after the March 22 attacks, the demonstration was postponed at the request of officials due to security worries. On Sunday, family members of the victims, paramedics, airport staff, and people from diverse religious backgrounds joined the march, bearing flowers to commemorate the deceased. The route went through Molenbeek, the district home to many of the suspected Brussels and Paris attackers, before ending at the makeshift memorial outside the city's stock exchange. Hassan Bousetta, an organizer of the march, told AFP that "When defenceless civilians, our fellow citizens, are murdered in a cowardly attack, all citizens must rise up to show their solidarity and abhorrence."

UEFA is weighing the implementation of goal-line technology, potentially alongside their existing system of additional assistant referees positioned near each goal. Discussions took place on Friday, and a final verdict is anticipated in January. This technology has been in use in the Premier League since the 2013-14 season and was utilized by FIFA during the 2014 World Cup. UEFA's general secretary, Gianni Infantino, conveyed a "positive" sentiment regarding its adoption at a press conference in Paris, while acknowledging certain "logistical challenges." He further mentioned that this topic has been under review for some time and that its introduction for Euro 2016 would extend to the Champions League and Europa League in the subsequent season, working in conjunction with the current five assistant referees. Despite the final decision being scheduled for January, the executive committee appears to be largely supportive of the proposed change.

Domino's Pizza Enterprises, the Sydney-listed company holding master franchise rights for Domino's in several countries, announced a 56.7% surge in net profit to A$45.6 million, compared to the prior year. The pizza chain credited this substantial growth to its internal expansion, highlighting its resilience amid global economic difficulties. Following its second profit upgrade since December, the company's stock value soared by more than 10% on Wednesday. Domino's also reported significant expansion in Japan, adding 48 stores in the six months to December, and confirmed that its Australian and New Zealand branches are on track to exceed 50 new store openings.

Carlos Brathwaite's stunning four consecutive sixes off Ben Stokes in the last over resulted in a painful loss for England to the West Indies. Nevertheless, Cook lauded Stokes as a remarkably gifted player and individual, expressing confidence in his ability to bounce back from the disappointment and achieve future success, such as a Test match score of 250. Cook recognized Brathwaite's phenomenal hitting, observing that although Stokes might regret his initial delivery, his second attempt wasn't significantly flawed but still went an impressive 94 meters. Speaking to BBC Essex, a clearly upset Cook confessed that he rarely gets emotional watching cricket. He regretted that the otherwise outstanding tournament concluded disappointingly, with the final over unfolding contrary to expectations. Cook's county team, Essex, is scheduled to embark on a new phase under their newly appointed coach, Chris Silverwood, on Sunday.

Law enforcement officials believe a man died from a heroin overdose, potentially exacerbated by the presence of fentanyl or carfentanyl, substances far more potent than standard heroin. He was found unresponsive by police at a home in Fitzwilliam, close to Wakefield, on Sunday and later passed away at a hospital. A 43-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the death. Det Ch Insp Stuart Spencer of West Yorkshire Police is urging heroin users, particularly those who purchase drugs from street vendors, to be extremely careful about the drugs they are using. This warning comes after a series of fatal overdoses in Hull, Barnsley, Leeds, and Normanton, West Yorkshire, linked to "deadly batches" of heroin. Previously, in March, Cleveland Police linked six deaths in Stockton-on-Tees to a particular batch of heroin.

Masai Graham won the "Joke of the Fringe" award with his witty line, "My dad suggested I register for a donor card, he's a man after my own heart." A panel of 10 judges selected the best jokes from the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, and the public then voted from a shortlist of jokes. The competition, sponsored by the Dave TV channel, has previously been won by comedians such as Tim Vine, Stewart Francis, and Zoe Lyon. Graham, who hails from West Bromwich and was a previous finalist in 2014 and 2015, was thrilled, remarking, "It's an incredible honour to land Joke of the Fringe. Not bad for someone from West Brom!" Stuart Mitchell secured second place with his joke: "Why is it old people say 'there's no place like home', yet when you put them in one..." The judging panel had to attend an average of 60 comedy shows.

Following a neighbor's concern for the well-being of children in her home, 31-year-old Erika Murray was arrested Thursday night. Detectives investigating the situation found the remains inside the house, which they described as filthy and overrun with pests. Ms. Murray pleaded not guilty to all charges on Friday, including fetal death concealment, witness intimidation, and child endangerment. Her lawyer, Keith Halpern, indicated a possible mental illness, saying after her court appearance, "People look for reasons in these situations... but mental illness doesn't always provide easy answers." Worcester district attorney spokesman Tim Connolly stated that police were initially called to the Blackstone home after a ten-year-old boy living there allegedly asked a neighbor, "How do you get a baby to stop crying?"

Jack Whitley, who was Chelsea's goalkeeper between 1907 and 1914, played for the club during their first ever season in the highest division of English football. When he died, he asked to be buried in Brompton Cemetery, even though he lived outside of London. Because it is believed his widow couldn't afford a proper gravestone, the Chelsea Supporters' Trust has started a crowdfunding effort to pay for one for Whitley. Rick Glanvill, Chelsea's official historian, stressed how important a headstone would be for Whitley, saying it would "mean a huge amount". Glanvill, who had been looking into the connections between the club and the cemetery, pointed out that it was unusually close to the football stadium, and that even though the club's original owner and a director were buried there, something was still missing.

Ben Stokes, the 24-year-old all-rounder, left the Sharjah match with his arm in a sling after diving to take a catch. While fielding at backward square leg, Stokes dived in an attempt to catch Sarfraz Ahmed's shot off Samit Patel. Stuart Broad of England told BBC Sport that they "knew immediately he was hurt when he landed." Broad expressed concern but noted the team's depth would allow them to adjust if Stokes couldn't continue. Stokes was clearly in pain after the fall and was seen leaving the field with his shirt used as a makeshift sling after receiving medical attention.

In April 2014, Boko Haram kidnapped 276 girls, but 21 were freed in October after Red Cross mediation. Despite being under government protection since their release, the girls' Christmas reunion in Chibok was marred by confinement to a politician's home, BBC sources revealed. They were barred from visiting their own houses or joining their families for Christmas church services. Although brought to a local official's house to see their parents, they were still forbidden from returning home. One heartbroken father, feeling it was like another captivity, exclaimed, "I can't believe my daughter is so near, yet can't come home," and was upset they couldn't even attend church on Christmas. Another parent recounted a soldier seizing his phone when he tried to photograph his daughter, saying, "I snapped a picture of myself and my daughter but the security guys came."

Banjong Pongphon, the mayor of Padang Besar, has been identified by police as a "key suspect" with "great influence" in the area where 26 bodies were discovered last week in mass graves. Padang Besar is a sub-district located in southern Songkhla province. The UN refugee agency reports that in the first three months of 2015, 25,000 migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh traveled on smugglers' boats, which is twice the number from the same period last year. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has indicated that smugglers' camps situated in the forests and plantations surrounding Padang Besar are the main destinations for these migrants. The cause of death for the bodies exhumed from the Songkhla graves is still unknown.

The police federation, which represents 1,000 officers in the county, has initiated a public awareness campaign, utilizing bus and newspaper ads, to warn that funding reductions are jeopardizing conventional policing strategies. They emphasize that Wiltshire Police has experienced a decrease of 153 officers since 2010. Despite Chief Constable Mike Veale's recognition of the cuts' effects, he insists on the force's commitment to local policing. The federation's "Cuts Have Consequences" campaign stresses that Wiltshire has the lowest number of officers per person in the UK. They caution that a 16% decrease in the workforce is leading to longer response times, making communities more susceptible to crime at night, and enabling drink-drivers to escape prosecution. The federation notes that the force has already reduced its budget by £17 million and is facing at least another £10 million in cuts. Federation chairman Mike White stated that personnel costs account for 80% of the policing budget.

A charity rugby match commemorating Edgar Mobbs, the former England international and Northampton Saints captain, will take place on January 24, 2015, at Olney Rugby Club. This event mirrors the England vs. Scotland game Mobbs organized on January 30, 1915, to recruit athletes for his World War One battalion. The commemorative match will pit players from the East Midlands against The 1st Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, alongside a game between Olney Ladies and the Army Women's XV. Mobbs, born in Northampton in 1882 and a former Olney player, captained Northampton Rugby Football Club from 1907. He earned seven England caps following his debut try against Australia in 1909 and progressed from private to battalion commander. He fought in significant battles, received the Distinguished Service Order and two mentions in Despatches, before his death on July 31 during the battle of Passchendale.

A charity report highlights a significant disparity: ten nations, accounting for just 2.5% of the world's GDP, are hosting more than half of the world's 21 million refugees. Amnesty International's Salil Shetty criticized wealthier nations, particularly the UK, for failing to accept their fair share of refugees. He pointed out that since 2011, the UK has resettled roughly 8,000 Syrian refugees, while the US has accepted only 12,000. UN data further reveals that China, Russia, and Gulf states have not resettled any Syrian refugees. Jordan, despite having a GDP only 1.2% the size of the UK's, hosts almost 655,000 Syrian refugees and a total of over 2.7 million refugees, making it the world's largest host country, followed by Turkey with over 2.5 million, Pakistan with 1.6 million, and Lebanon with over 1.5 million.

A man was caught on CCTV footage on Monday afternoon outside Jonathan Gwyer's home in Whitstable, dumping the contents of his food waste bin into the regular trash bin after looking through it. Serco, the waste disposal firm, apologized for the "completely unacceptable" behavior of one of its agency workers. Gwyer, who lives on Colombia Avenue, voiced his dismay, feeling his recycling was pointless and wondering why waste separation was necessary. Although he understands the convenience of using just one bin, he mainly blamed Serco, not the worker, understanding the job's difficulties, and mentioned observing more hurried and disorganized actions from the workers lately. Serco released a statement reiterating their dedication to recycling.

To prevent local councils from pursuing unpaid poll tax, the Community Charge Debt bill establishes a cutoff date. Following the Scottish independence referendum, increased voter registration led to larger electoral rolls, which were then utilized to find individuals with outstanding poll tax debts. The Scottish government has promised to reimburse local councils for this effort. The poll tax, or community charge, was implemented in Scotland in 1989 by Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government, preceding the rest of the UK, and abolished in 1993 after a four-year run. Replacing the existing rates system, this unpopular tax sparked significant public protests. Scottish local authorities have seen a decline in the total amount of recovered poll tax arrears, dropping below £350,000 in 2013-14, with some councils ceasing debt recovery. Deputy First Minister John Swinney characterized the poll tax as a "hated levy" that caused hardship in Scottish communities and was broadly denounced as an impractical and universally disliked tax.

Although both parties agreed to work together to fight extremism and improve the economy, expectations for a complete resolution between them lessened when they issued individual statements on Wednesday. Libya has experienced instability since the ousting of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. Fayez Sarraj, head of the UN-backed government, and his rival Khalifa Haftar have been in discussions in the United Arab Emirates this week. Haftar, who commands the Libyan National Army (LNA) and controls eastern Libya, has opposed international efforts to settle the conflict, declining to acknowledge Sarraj's UN-supported Government of National Accord (GNA) since it was established in 2015. A source close to the GNA leadership told Reuters that the two sides initially attempted to create a joint statement on Wednesday before opting to release separate ones. Both statements urged an end to Libya's political and economic crises.

In July 2014, a woman from Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, persistently reported Craig Hutsby to the police for threats and bail breaches, but he subsequently raped her the following month. An IPCC report later revealed that this rape could have been prevented had arrest forms been completed without delay. Detective Superintendent Rachel Walker confirmed that misconduct meetings were held with officers. The IPCC determined that PC Sofi Essex was responsible for misconduct due to her failure to prepare the required "arrest package"—the necessary documentation for initiating an arrest—when asked to do so. According to the IPCC, this delay in completing the paperwork prevented any action to find and arrest Craig Hutsby before the rape occurred. Furthermore, the IPCC concluded that PC Joseph Lovelock was also guilty of misconduct for incorrectly filling out a form for the victim, leading to a failure to identify her as being at high risk and implement suitable safeguards.

In front of 15,000 spectators in Berlin, SKT1 triumphed over the Koo Tigers from South Korea to seize the championship and the $1 million prize (£650,000). SKT1 won the final match 3-1, with Koo Tigers being the only team able to win even a single game against them throughout the entire tournament. Following the win, Gyeong-hwan Jang of SKT1 stated, "We have a strong track record against Koo, having faced them numerous times. We noticed their strategies remained largely unchanged over the past year, and our predictions were accurate." Jang, known as Marin, was named the most valuable player due to his vital role in securing SKT1's second championship, achieved despite only two players remaining from their 2013 winning team.

Tatenda Taibu, the 32-year-old former Zimbabwe player with 28 Test and 150 ODI appearances before retiring in 2012, surprisingly contacted Hightown Cricket Club. Nick Gordon, Hightown's publicity officer, initially dismissed it as a joke, saying, "I thought it was a hoax when he explained who he was." After confirming Taibu's identity through Zimbabwean cricket connections, negotiations advanced, leading Gordon to admit, "It's a real coup for us." The ex-wicketkeeper-batsman is now expected to make his debut for the Second Division side against Alder on April 24. Gordon revealed to BBC Radio Merseyside that Taibu responded to the club's advertisement for an overseas player, adding, "It's not every day that a club like Hightown St Mary's signs a player like Tatenda," highlighting the unexpected nature of the signing. "I had to do a double take, it was so unusual."

Marking the first such encounter since the normalization of relations twenty years ago, this meeting saw President Obama affirm the growing partnership between the US and Vietnam, despite their differing political systems. Analysts believe this deepening relationship serves as a counterbalance to China's increasing influence. Occurring during the 40th anniversary of the Vietnam War's end, Obama recognized the difficult past and remaining political disagreements, while underscoring the development of a mutually beneficial and respectful relationship. Mr. Trong described the talks as "cordial, constructive, positive, and frank," stressing the evolution from enemies to friends and comprehensive partners, expressing optimism for continued progress and inviting Obama to visit Vietnam.

Acknowledging the gravity of the threat posed by al-Shabab, the official highlighted a recent video released by the Somalia-based group that incites attacks on shopping centers in the US, Canada, and the UK. He recalled al-Shabab's prior claim of responsibility for the 2013 Westgate mall attack in Nairobi, which caused 67 deaths. In an interview with CNN, he characterized the threat as "a new phase" of terrorism, marked by more attacks by "independent actors in their homelands." He stressed the importance of taking seriously any terrorist group's call for attacks on specific targets but noted that he was not advising people to stay away from the malls mentioned by the militants. The video featured a masked man with a British accent urging al-Shabab supporters to attack "American or..." targets.

After talks with Irish Prime Minister Enda Kenny, the Prime Minister described the UK and Ireland as "close friends." Kenny voiced his pleasure with the deepening connection between their countries. Cameron is set to join the Queen and Duke of Edinburgh at a state dinner during their historic four-day visit—the first by a British monarch since Irish independence. Cameron stressed that the Queen's presence underscores the possibility of an even more robust relationship, built on trade, investment, economic bonds, and collaborative prospects for neighboring allies. He also acknowledged the Queen's "enormous sensitivity" to the intricate shared history of the UK and Ireland. Although Cameron and Kenny met previously in Downing Street in April, this is their first meeting in Ireland since Kenny became Prime Minister in March.

The @RogueNASA account describes itself as the "unofficial 'Resistance' team of NASA," emphasizing that it is not an official NASA account or managed by government staff, but provides factual information with a touch of irony. BBC News contacted @ActualEPAFacts, a rogue Environmental Protection Agency account, which stated its goal was to continue disseminating factual information about climate change and other scientific studies during the Trump administration. News reports suggest that the Trump administration has tried to limit public communication from some government agencies, including the EPA. The official EPA Twitter account has been dormant since January 19, the day before Mr. Trump's inauguration.

While the Labour party officially supports remaining in the EU, Jeremy Corbyn, a known EU critic, has been urged to champion the cause more forcefully. Worried MPs warned that the referendum could be "lost" without a more enthusiastic pro-EU stance from Labour. His spokesperson indicated he will soon give a "big" speech on the matter. During a visit to Dagenham, Corbyn admitted the EU has flaws that need addressing, but emphasized the importance of European unity in Labour's current campaign. He stated Labour is focusing on "social justice across Europe," citing the social chapter on workers' rights and the Working Time Directive. Corbyn also mentioned seeking support from socialist parties across Europe. Notably, during his leadership campaign, Corbyn hadn't ruled out the possibility of.

Matthew Eteson, 42, is on trial at Preston Crown Court, accused of manslaughter by gross negligence for the deaths of Kelly Webster, 36, and her daughter, Lauren Thornton. The prosecution, led by Graham Reeds QC, asserts that the tragedy occurred on April 1, 2013, during an Easter bank holiday trip to Windermere. Eteson allegedly relocated a generator from the boat's deck and used it to power a 1kW fan heater inside the cabin where the victims were sleeping. The court was informed that the carbon monoxide detectors were non-functional, failing to alert the mother and daughter from Leyland, Lancashire, to the accumulating poisonous gas. They were found dead in their beds aboard the Arniston, a used Bayliner 285 motor cruiser, with fatal levels of carbon monoxide in their bodies.

While performing standard upkeep on Reactor Three, EDF Energy detected fissures in three graphite bricks. The company clarified that this issue, akin to "keyway root cracking" identified in the other reactor the previous year, presents no danger to safety and does not impede the reactor's function. EDF Energy explained that the disclosure aims to highlight their commitment to open communication and transparency. Station director Colin Weir stressed that nuclear safety remains the company's paramount concern, and they maintain considerable safety buffers, which include allowances for the graphite bricks. He further noted that the permitted degree of cracking is substantially less than what would lead to any adverse effects.

The company behind the London Array wind farm has initiated a three-year study to evaluate how additional turbines could affect red-throated divers. Their original proposal envisioned expanding the wind farm, located off the coasts of Kent and Essex, to encompass 341 turbines. This area provides winter refuge for around 6,500 red-throated divers, representing at least a third of the UK's overall population. London Array has formally requested The Crown Estate to terminate the lease for the second phase area and has also relinquished the reserved grid capacity at the National Grid substation in Graveney, Kent. Approved in 2006, the wind farm project, situated 10 miles north of Ramsgate, Kent, was conditional on safeguarding red-throated divers during the phase two expansion, which intended to add 166 turbines. The RSPB had previously expressed worries that the extension might displace the bird population from the outer Thames estuary. According to Mike, the general manager of London Array,

If Mr. McClarty had returned to the UUP, they would have gained two executive positions. His decision to remain independent means they retain only one, automatically awarding Alliance a seat. McClarty explained that he was fulfilling a promise to many constituents who urged him to stay independent. While recognizing his leverage to potentially obtain a ministerial role, he insisted his choice was not for personal gain. He also voiced concerns about the UUP's structure, characterizing it as a loosely connected group of associations without unified control. BBC's Gareth Gordon pointed out that McClarty, who left the Ulster Unionists in January following his deselection, denied that revenge played a part in his decision, adding that this outcome would certainly be a blow to his previous party.

Robert Hannigan, who had been the director of GCHQ since 2014, declared his departure, stating it was for family reasons. While proud of what he achieved, he mentioned that his twenty years of public service had taken a toll on his family life. Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson recognized Hannigan's contributions to updating national security protections against terrorism while at GCHQ. Before heading GCHQ, Hannigan was the director general of defense and intelligence at the Foreign Office. In his resignation letter, he emphasized the lives GCHQ had saved, both in the UK and abroad, but concluded that it was time for a change in leadership, suggesting a new director should take over.

IHS reported that the territory controlled by IS, since its declaration of a "caliphate" two years earlier, had shrunk to 68,300 sq km (26,370 sq miles). This loss of land has led IS to intensify its attacks on civilians in the Middle East and Europe, a pattern that is expected to persist, the report indicated. A suicide bombing by IS in Baghdad the week before resulted in almost 300 deaths, shortly after the Iraqi government proclaimed the full liberation of Falluja, situated west of the capital. IHS further stated that IS held around 90,800 sq km of Iraqi and Syrian territory in January 2015, six months after declaring its caliphate. David Poole, 38, pleaded guilty at Cardiff Crown Court to trapping 27-year-old Adnan Khalid, who was accused of grooming a 14-year-old. Poole was charged with giving false evidence during the trial of Khalid, from Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taff. Judge Thomas Crowther QC acquitted Khalid and reprimanded H Division, the paedophile hunter group Poole founded, for causing the trial's failure. Poole, of Hereford, created a fake profile named Chloe on Plenty of Fish, pretending to be a 14-year-old, and set up a meeting with Khalid in Cardiff after WhatsApp conversations, secretly recording it. Khalid, who denied the charges, stated he thought he was talking to a woman over 18. Poole's lateness to court and subsequent false statement about providing photographic evidence to the police prompted Judge Crowther's criticism.

Jamie Vardy, 29, postponed his wedding twice, initially last year and then from June, to play in Euro 2016. England manager Roy Hodgson understood Vardy's need for a wedding break. Following his goal that secured England's 2-1 win against Turkey on Sunday, Vardy confirmed he would be off on Wednesday but would return to training afterward. Hodgson affirmed Vardy's place in the squad, while also noting the importance of evaluating other players. Vardy, who scored 24 Premier League goals for Leicester's title-winning season, started on the left of the attacking front three against Turkey at the Etihad Stadium, later moving to the center and scoring the winning goal after Harry Kane's initial score.

To reduce doctor visits and overuse of antibiotics, NHS England has launched a walk-in service that aims to alleviate pressure on GPs and potentially save the NHS millions each year. Pharmacies, however, worry that funding cuts could jeopardize the program's effectiveness. The Sore Throat Test and Treat service, previously piloted in 35 Boots pharmacies, differentiates between viral infections, which do not respond to antibiotics, and bacterial infections. The service uses a rapid throat swab test, analyzing tongue sugars to provide results in five minutes, allowing pharmacists to directly prescribe antibiotics to patients who need them, bypassing the need for a GP appointment. NHS chief executive Simon Stevens has announced the nationwide rollout of the program next year, with Dr. Adam Roberts, a University College London microbiologist specializing in antibiotic resistance, calling it "quite an innovative step."

The ceasefire in Eastern Ghouta commenced following Russia's declaration of a deal with "moderate" rebels to de-escalate the conflict, though analysts question how well it can be enforced. Eastern Ghouta was previously designated as one of four "de-escalation zones" in a May agreement involving Russia, Iran, and Turkey. The Syrian army stated that the truce began at noon local time on Saturday (09:00 GMT), cautioning that any breaches would be met with a "suitable" response. Faylaq al-Rahman, a rebel faction, hailed the pause in fighting and urged the government to respect it. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights noted some isolated shelling after the ceasefire came into effect, but no major clashes. This development occurred after Russia announced a separate agreement with rebels in Cairo concerning the operational aspects of the safe zone.

An A320 pilot narrowly avoided a mid-air collision with a white quadcopter drone south of Brookmans Park in August, reporting the drone "flashed past" the aircraft. The UK Airprox Board concluded the near miss was only averted by chance due to lack of reaction time. Air traffic control verified the A320 pilot's report of an object passing overhead north of Potters Bar around 18:45 BST on August 15, 2016. Despite air traffic control's record of another aircraft passing above, the pilot described the object as under a meter in size, with a red and white body and red and blue stripes on two rotor arms. Drone operators are legally required to comply with the Air Navigation Order (ANO) 2016 articles regarding small unmanned aircraft operation.

The hashtag #penuriecarburantdansunfilm, or "fuel shortage in a film," became a top trending topic on French Twitter on Tuesday, exceeding 5,000 tweets. This spike occurred after strikes affected all eight of France's oil refineries in response to new labor legislation. Around 20% of French gas stations are reportedly facing fuel exhaustion or limited supplies. French social media users alluded to films like Total Recall, a science fiction movie with iterations in 1990 and 2012, subtly referencing the French oil and gas company, Total. Additionally, some users playfully modified film titles, for example, changing Pulp Fiction to Pump Friction, to reflect the fuel crisis.

After uncovering cheating involving 54 student officers, a probe at the Garverville college in east Belfast exposed a "pseudo-militaristic" atmosphere with an overemphasis on punitive actions. In response, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has committed to enacting 50 suggested improvements. Chief Constable George Hamilton and high-ranking PSNI leaders are slated to confer with the Policing Board to deliberate on a strategy for resolving the highlighted problems. Several immediate adjustments have been implemented within the 22-week training curriculum, including eliminating the practice of marching students between locations and ceasing military-style "show parades" as a form of discipline. Furthermore, student groups will now be referred to as "classes" rather than "squads." The PSNI's plan details 34 modifications intended to be finalized by the close of March of the subsequent year.

The royal tour began at the Seamus Heaney Homeplace in Bellaghy, allowing the couple to meet members of the poet's family. Their schedule encompasses visits to Londonderry, Belfast, and County Down. In Bellaghy, they toured the visitor's centre, a key source of inspiration for much of Heaney's celebrated poetry. Prince Charles, a known admirer of the Nobel Prize winner, had previously encountered Heaney on multiple occasions. After Bellaghy, they visited the North West Cancer Centre at Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry, where they spoke with personnel and patients. The day concluded with their attendance at a musical performance at Hillsborough Castle in County Down on Tuesday evening.

Built in 1908, the single-lane swing bridge over the River Weaver Navigation in Northwich is the subject of a campaign for upgrades. Local parish councillors and MP George Osborne are advocating for the improvements, citing "mayhem" during rush hour. Cheshire West and Chester Council has responded by scheduling a feasibility study. The Grade II listed Winnington Turn Bridge, an early electrically operated swing bridge on the A533 leading to the M56, is a major source of congestion. Barnton Parish Council Chair Dilys Hooper notes that delays can reach 40 minutes during peak times, leading to chaotic conditions. With at least 4,300 new homes planned for the Northwich vicinity, Ms. Hooper predicts increased pressure on the bridge's ability to handle traffic.

On Monday night, eight men posing as police officers broke through the airport perimeter and entered a plane scheduled to depart for Switzerland. From the cargo area, they stole approximately $50 million (Â£32 million; 37 million euros) in gems before escaping through the same breach. Soon after, a torched vehicle was found close to the airport. Caroline De Wolf of the Antwerp World Diamond Centre characterized the value of the stolen gems as "a gigantic sum." While early reports suggested a larger amount, with Belgian state broadcaster putting it at 350 million euros ($468 million), an anonymous Antwerp center representative called the heist "one of the biggest" on record, verifying that the stolen goods were "rough stones" being transported from Antwerp, the world's primary diamond trading hub, to Zurich.

Cardiff held Wales' largest deficit in 2010, totaling £494 million or £1,450 per resident, while Merthyr Tydfil's per capita deficit of £2,268 was the highest in the UK. Councils challenged the report, claiming they had already tackled pension affordability issues. The Taxpayers Alliance analyzed 101 UK local government pension schemes, utilizing 2010-11 financial reports and actuarial projections to assess their funding levels. The Alliance contended that these final salary schemes were "inflexible and too expensive" and needed immediate reform, urging councils to take corrective measures.

The delayed 2012 badger cull cost £2.5 million, with subsequent expenses of £9.8 million in 2013 and £4.5 million in 2014. Critics have labeled the cull policy a "disastrous" and growing financial strain on taxpayers. Defra reported a 50% reduction in operational costs between 2013 and 2014, attributed to increased farmer contributions. Bovine TB, a significant threat to cattle farming spread by badgers, necessitates routine cattle testing and the culling of infected animals; in 2014, 26,413 TB-positive cattle were culled in England. The effectiveness of the badger culls in curbing TB transmission and the ethical implications of nighttime badger shootings have raised concerns. These figures were revealed by The [Organization Name] via a Freedom of Information request.

Christopher Kelly, aged 40, killed 51-year-old Dorothy Beattie by strangulation at her Dunoon, Argyll and Bute home on May 22nd. The High Court in Glasgow heard that the attack was triggered by an insult Ms. Beattie allegedly made about Kelly's children. Kelly, who confessed to a doctor leading to his apprehension, initially faced a murder charge but pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of culpable homicide. The court learned that Kelly had previously been a support worker for Ms. Beattie, who suffered from various health problems, including seizures. The divorced mother and Kelly became friends and often socialized. However, he assaulted her at her residence after she allegedly made "derogatory" remarks about his children, strangling her before leaving and later returning to find her dead.

State Prosecutor Marilyn Mosby announced revised charges on Thursday in the Freddie Gray case, upholding the second-degree murder charge. Gray's death, a week after suffering a severe spinal injury in police custody in April, sparked extensive demonstrations, followed by riots and looting in Baltimore. Mosby stated that adjusting charges during an ongoing investigation is a standard and suitable procedure as new evidence emerges. Although the grand jury chose not to indict on the false imprisonment charges initially brought by Mosby, who claimed Gray's arrest was illegal, they added new reckless endangerment charges not present in the initial announcement three weeks earlier. Mosby insists Gray's neck was broken while being handcuffed and placed in a police van, and that officers ignored his repeated pleas for assistance.

The family of Baboucarr Ceesay, a 21-year-old Gambian feared dead after a shipwreck off the Libyan coast on Sunday, are mourning his loss. His aunt, Jessica Sey of Cheltenham, voiced the family's despair, lamenting the lack of accountability and calling for greater awareness of the dangers migrants face. She insisted that those who profit from exploiting migrants "have got to be held to account." Mrs. Sey highlighted the local impact of this global issue, noting her nephew's fatal journey to the UK was "a desperate way out." Although a gifted football player with a good life in Gambia, his desire for a better life in Europe led him and a friend to take a boat from Banjul to Guinea before crossing the Sahara on a dangerous voyage.

An AI algorithm has surpassed BBC pundit Mark Lawrenson's football predictions for the last two seasons, leading its developers to invite fantasy football players to compete against it. The researchers believe this algorithm could help players build better fantasy teams. Fantasy football, invented in 1971 in the UK by Bernie Donnelly, allows users to create virtual teams of actual footballers and score points based on those players' real-world performance. What began as a niche hobby has grown into a significant online business, featuring ad-supported platforms, downloadable applications, and wagering options. In the free Fantasy Premier League salary cap game, managers can now measure their skills against Squadguru's AI in the "Challenge the Squadguru" league.

Reports indicate the explosion took place while people were waiting in line for food at the camp, which shelters those displaced by conflict in the tribal areas near Afghanistan, a known haven for Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters. Police suggest the camp also harbors some of these militants. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack, which is uncommon for refugee camps in Pakistan, despite long-standing concerns about militant infiltration in Jalozai and other camps. The BBC's M Ilyas Khan in Islamabad notes that a government-backed tribal force recently arrested individuals linked to the militant group Lashkar-e-Islam, leading police to suspect the bombing was an act of revenge. Live broadcasts showed ambulances taking victims to hospitals as police investigated the bomb's crater amid the wreckage.

A city council report stated that the July 2015 yacht races boosted tourism and enhanced the city's reputation, but also highlighted problems such as unclear spectator ticketing and unsightly steel barriers. A key change for the next event is the elimination of evening entertainment. The four-day weekend event in July 2015, organized by TeamOrigin Events, marked the debut of the sailing series, with Sir Ben Ainslie Racing (BAR) launching Britain's bid for the 35th America's Cup. While Saturday's races attracted approximately 100,000 spectators, Sunday's races were canceled due to adverse weather conditions, resulting in the evacuation of public viewing zones. The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge were among the disappointed attendees, and social media users expressed dissatisfaction with spectator facilities.

Security forces employed tear gas and live rounds to break up a largely Shia Muslim protest against government corruption and poor security. While a curfew was initially imposed in Baghdad, it has since been rescinded. This is the second time this month that protesters have forced their way into the city's government zone. Shia cleric Moqtada Sadr condemned the harsh crackdown, voicing his support for the demonstrators' "peaceful [and] spontaneous revolt." At least 50 protesters are reported to have been injured. The protesters allege governmental inaction on essential reforms amidst the ongoing fight against the Islamic State group (IS) and declining oil revenues. The Sunni jihadist group continues to control territory in western and northern Iraq and has claimed responsibility for several recent deadly attacks. Some protesters managed to gain entry to the prime minister's office and the parliament building. Baghdad's Green Zone houses the parliament, key government buildings, and various foreign embassies.

Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister, Peter O'Neill, revealed in a public announcement that he met with Australia's Immigration Minister, Peter Dutton, in Port Moresby, and they jointly agreed to close the Manus Island Regional Processing Centre. This decision is a consequence of the PNG Supreme Court's April decision deeming the detention of asylum seekers and refugees there as unconstitutional. Although the center, which currently houses 854 men, will not close immediately, Prime Minister O'Neill stated that different options are being considered and implemented. He highlighted the importance of a careful and measured strategy that takes into account the interests of Papua New Guineans along with the well-being of the asylum seekers and refugees. It is important to remember that Australia's policy involves transferring asylum seekers arriving by boat to offshore detention centers.

BBC Three's online platform is set to deliver weekly coverage of the Gfinity Elite Series, a competition featuring 160 gamers vying for a £225,000 prize pool before live crowds. Despite e-sports' already significant online audience, an expert suggests the BBC's participation could attract new viewers. The deal encompasses broadcasts of exclusive content from the Gfinity tournament held in west London, showcasing gamers competing in Street Fighter V, Counter Strike: Global Offensive, and Rocket League. While Twitch and YouTube currently lead the e-sports streaming market, traditional television channels, such as Ginx in the UK, are also broadcasting events. The BBC asserts that its Gfinity coverage will be "on a much larger scale" than its previous e-sports highlights programming, according to IHS analyst Piers Harding-Rolls.

This interactive display has the ability to replicate a smartphone's touchscreen, a full computer keyboard, or even piano keys. In addition, the laser projector can project images and videos onto walls. The Smart Cast phone, along with a new smartwatch, was unveiled at Lenovo's Tech World conference in Beijing. Lenovo claims its laser projector, a compact 34mm x 26mm x 5mm, removes the necessity for focusing, ensuring sharp visuals on walls or other flat areas. A demo video shows how rotating the lens mount changes the device from a standard wall projector to "surface mode," allowing projection onto surfaces.

A Metropolitan Police Federation survey gauging officer opinions on firearms due to persistent terrorism threats found that only 6% of the 11,000 participants believed the number of armed officers was sufficient, even with the Met's intention to recruit an additional 600. Given that the UK's international terrorism threat level has remained at "severe" since August 2014, the survey showed that 43% desired more specialist firearm officers, 26% felt all officers should be regularly armed, and 12% would refuse to carry a firearm. The data also highlighted 2,139 authorized firearms officers (6.7% of the total police force), 3,974 police firearms operations between March 2015 and March 2016, and 7 instances where police firearms were discharged in 2015-16. There was strong support for Tasers, with 75% supporting universal access. The poll also investigated if the presence of armed police provided reassurance.

Geraint Thomas, aged 28, is a key component of Team Sky's strategy to help Chris Froome secure his second straight Tour de France title. Thomas voiced apprehension about the dangerous cobblestone sectors, particularly given Froome's X-ray after a stage four crash. He pointed out how rain could instantly ruin a rider's chances, highlighting the heartbreak after a year's preparation. Thomas is hoping for dry weather to avoid crashes. Froome's fall happened early in the 163.5km stage four due to contact with another rider's wheel in the pack. Although the 29-year-old suffered a grazed hip and wrist, he was able to continue racing after receiving treatment. With Marcel Kittel winning the stage, Froome is currently seventh overall, trailing leader Vincenzo Nibali by a mere two seconds.

The Supreme Court is expected to rule by the end of June in a case concerning a Virginia school district's policy preventing a transgender student, assigned female at birth, from using the boys' restroom. The even number of justices, due to Antonin Scalia's death, raises the possibility of a 4-4 split decision. The core of the dispute lies in differing approaches among school districts nationwide regarding bathroom access for transgender students, often tied to birth certificates. Gloucester County, Virginia, appealed to the Supreme Court, resulting in a stay of a lower court order that had allowed transgender student Gavin Grimm to use the male restrooms. Grimm, who identifies as male, sued the school board after publicly coming out as transgender during his freshman year.

Angus Campbell, head of the Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, drew attention to the unfair airfare prices, mentioning that the airline serving Stornoway had cheaper options for destinations like the Algarve. A Facebook campaign protesting this situation has attracted significant support, with over 11,000 "likes." Loganair, Flybe's collaborator for island routes, justified its pricing structure by mentioning reduced fares for specific groups, including children, students, hospital patients, and island inhabitants. Campbell stressed that lowering air travel expenses is a central goal of Our Islands Our Future, a program designed to achieve increased self-governance for the Shetland, Orkney, and Western Isles councils. He underscored the problem of expensive flights, giving the example of a £351 round-trip fare from Stornoway to Glasgow on Flybe, noting that similar flights in other regions were less costly.

In 2012, the Northern Echo reported that Cleveland Police allegedly tried to monitor the communications of six people, including its journalists, a staffer, and a lawyer, an allegation stemming from a front-page story in the paper. The police force has not commented to the BBC, but the Police Federation has lodged a complaint with the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC). The Echo alleges the police used the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA), meant for crime or public safety surveillance, to identify the source of information for a story about institutionalized racism within the force, which was based on an internal police report. A Cleveland Police spokeswoman told the paper she could "neither confirm nor deny" if a RIPA application was used to monitor the phone activity of three journalists, a police officer, a solicitor, and the chairman of the Cleveland Police Federation at the time.

Research on employees and managers showed that a quarter of new fathers took no paternity leave at all, and fewer than 10% took more than the statutory two weeks. The Institute of Leadership & Management (ILM), who carried out the study, blamed this on ingrained employer prejudice and financial worries for new fathers. Despite the government's introduction of shared parental leave planned for April 2015, the ILM's results imply it will have little effect unless employer perceptions are challenged. Charles Elvin, ILM's chief executive, highlighted the importance of shared parental leave for women's career progression, but the research reveals cultural barriers preventing fathers from using both statutory and extra leave, underscoring a continuing "cultural expectation" that women are the main caregivers.

On March 14th, Irish Coastguard Rescue Helicopter 116 tragically crashed, carrying four individuals. While Captain Dara Fitzpatrick was rescued from the water, she subsequently passed away. The search continues for the remaining crew, with divers resuming their efforts on Friday following an improvement in weather. Garda Superintendent Tony Healy confirmed that divers are "actively working" on the seabed and will conclude their dives at nightfall, reiterating that recovering the crew remains the top priority. Jurgen Whyte, the IAAIU's chief inspector, reported that the data recorder was successfully recovered at 4:30 PM from the seabed near Blackrock. This recorder will be taken to Dublin before being sent to the UK's air accident investigation branch for analysis.

The "Vermeer's Women: Secrets and Silence" exhibition has drawn impressive crowds, with over 130,000 visitors since its October debut. A major highlight is Vermeer's diminutive masterpiece, "The Lacemaker," on loan from The Louvre and making its UK debut. Responding to the exhibition's immense popularity, the museum will extend its hours during the final two weeks. Curator Betsy Wiseman credits "The Lacemaker" as a primary driver of this success, highlighting its rarity as a loan from The Louvre, who consider it almost as important as the Mona Lisa. The exhibition also features significant pieces such as "A Lady At The Virginals With A Gentleman (The Music Lesson)" from The Royal Collection and "A Young Woman Seated At A Virginal" from London's National Gallery.

Helen Bailey, 51, was found dead in a cesspool at her Royston, Hertfordshire home in July 2016, after disappearing on April 11th. Her fiance, Ian Stewart, denies murdering her. At St Albans Crown Court, Edward Farmer initially testified he saw Bailey in a car in Broadstairs, Kent, between mid-April and June, but later admitted the sighting could have been earlier. Farmer claimed he saw Bailey alone on Charlotte Street, near her holiday home, "driving what looked to be a Range Rover or that type of 4x4, a dark colour," which the court heard contradicted the defense's claim that two violent men abducted her and took her to Broadstairs. Farmer estimated the sighting occurred "about five, maybe six weeks prior to the police interview" when questioned about the date.

Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting showed policymakers were worried about stock market fluctuations and global economic fragility. However, they were reluctant to express these concerns openly to avoid potential misinterpretations. The officials remained optimistic about the US economy's fundamental health, a key factor in their decision to end quantitative easing (QE), a bond-buying program designed to keep long-term interest rates low and encourage spending. The meeting summary indicated a general consensus that the economy was robust enough to continue moving toward full employment, thus justifying the QE program's termination. The US markets reacted calmly to the news, with the Dow Jones briefly increasing before falling back down.

Robin Waistell claimed that the unsalability of his Maesteg house was a direct result of the rail authority's inaction regarding the rampant knotweed infestation on the adjacent embankment. This case was seen as potentially setting a precedent for homeowners impacted by knotweed originating from railway property. Network Rail announced they would thoroughly review the judgment. Reportedly, the rail organization's request for immediate appeal was rejected. After losing the Cardiff case to Mr. Waistell and his neighbor, Network Rail is likely to incur legal costs totaling a substantial sum. Mr. Waistell, a 70-year-old widower, had moved to the bungalow from Spain after his wife passed away, planning to eventually return, but the knotweed spreading from Network Rail's land prevented him from selling his home.

Rex Tillerson's confirmation hearing included comments likely to worsen relations with Beijing, focusing on China's creation of artificial islands on contested reefs. These waters are subject to overlapping claims, and recent analysis indicates potential military deployments on some islands. Tillerson likened China's actions to Russia's Crimea annexation before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. He argued the US must firmly demand China cease island construction and block access to them. China's island-building has caused regional unease, as Beijing claims nearly all of the South China Sea, conflicting with claims from Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia, and Brunei. While an international court sided against China's claims in July, ruling in favor of a case brought by the Philippines, Beijing has dismissed the decision.

Aberdeen City Council announced it may issue index-linked bonds in the future, contingent on market conditions. Aberdeen, already the first Scottish council with a credit rating (Aa2 by Moody's), intends to use the bond proceeds to support its £1 billion capital plan. Council leader Jennifer Laing described the potential bond issue as a historic moment for the city, marking another first for a Scottish local authority following its credit rating. She added that this forward-thinking capital funding strategy underscores their dedication to protecting the revenue budget, which is vital for providing public services.

In Chicago, American Gwen Jorgensen triumphed, with Stanford taking second place and Holland finishing third. Jorgensen's strong running performance propelled her to victory, marking her 15th consecutive win and securing her second world title in a row. Stanford, a former world champion representing Wales, confessed to feeling pressure due to the demanding qualification criteria. Holland conveyed her delight in achieving a podium finish, particularly after a breakaway with only two other athletes. Jorgensen's total time for the 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride, and 10km run was 1 hour, 55 minutes, and 36 seconds. Stanford, the second Welsh woman to qualify for Rio after Hannah Mills, crossed the finish line 29 seconds later.

GMB Scotland claims that the jobs of its offshore workers are at risk, and union leaders will seek permission from the regional committee to hold a strike vote for members under the Offshore Contractors Agreement, echoing a recent announcement by Unite. These actions are a reaction to job cuts and wage reductions planned by several North Sea oil and gas firms due to persistently low oil prices. GMB's decision comes after failed talks on Friday between the two unions and the Offshore Contractors Association (OCA), representing offshore contractors. The Offshore Contractors Agreement covers workers in mechanical, electrical, construction, maintenance, design, project engineering, fabrication, decommissioning, and related fields. GMB Scotland's regional officer, John Kelly, accused certain oil companies and contractors of "blatant opportunism" in their attempts to severely weaken workforce terms and conditions.

In the first half, Walsall threatened more, but Albion's Jon McLaughlin blocked efforts from Paul Downing and Romaine Sawyers. Burton's Stuart Beavon managed to get into Walsall's box, but his shot went wide. After Wigan's win against Bury, Albion's lead at the top narrows to two points, with Walsall holding steady in fourth. Burton Albion's manager, Nigel Clough, told BBC Radio Derby that the close-fought match, with few opportunities, was no classic. He valued the clean sheet and point, acknowledging better passing in their Monday night performance, but stressed the team's regained solidity and strong defense.
